newsitem.title: UK: UK managers unhappy with budget, poll shows.
newsitem.headline: UK managers unhappy with budget, poll shows.

text.p: Around half of Britain's managers believe the November budget will not be good for business and over half think it had more to do with short-term political aims than long-term economic goals, the Institute of Management said.

In a survey of 312 managers, it found that 69 percent did not believe the government could achieve a planned seven percent cut in spending, and more than half thought underlying inflation in 1997 would be above the government's 2.5 percent target.
A clear majority also doubted the government's ability to meet its targets for the budget deficit and for GDP growth.

"Managers do not share the Chancellor's breezy confidence about the UK economy. A shiver runs up their spines as they face the chilling prospect of rising interest rates and inflation," the Institute's director-general, Roger Young, said.
In his November 26 budget, Chancellor Kenneth Clarke cut the basic income tax rate by one percentage point to 23 percent.
The poll, conducted over the past week, showed 60 percent of managers believed the cut in income tax was not justified, with over half saying it was likely to fuel inflation.
As many as 72 percent expected interest rates to rise before the election, due by May 22 next year, while only a quarter expected a reduction in corporate taxes to benefit them.
